question.value: How does the molecular Kennicutt-Schmidt (mK-S) star formation law behave on 500 pc scales across different surface brightness and morphological regimes in the early-stage luminous infrared galaxy merger Arp 240?

evidence.quote: We study SF and molecular gas (MG) distribution in the early-stage luminous infrared galaxy merger Arp240 (NGC5257-8).
In this study, we explore the mK-S law for sub-kpc regions within a system of two massive galaxies that are in the early stage of their merger.
Our analysis of molecular gas was conducted using the CO ($2\rightarrow1$) transition, employing ALMA pipeline-calibrated datasets (ID 2015.1.00804.S, PI: Kazimierz Sliwa).
This paper makes use of the following ALMA data: ADS/JAO.ALMA$\#$2015.1.00804.S.

key_parameters.value: Radio continuum threshold: 3-sigma; CO(2->1) threshold: > 2-sigma across at least 9 consecutive channels

evidence.quote: For region selection, we applied a threshold of three times the rms noise value (3-$\sigma$) to each radio continuum image at each frequency band.

analysis_steps.goal: Derive molecular gas surface density (Sigma_H2), SFE, and depletion time (t_d)

method.value: Extract CO(2-1) line profiles per hexagon, sum over channels multiplied by 3 km s^-1 channel width, convert to L'_CO(1-0), multiply by alpha_CO to get M_H2, divide by beam area in pc^2 for Sigma_H2, and compute SFE = Sigma_SFR / Sigma_H2 and t_d = 1 / SFE.

evidence.quote: To calculate $S_{CO}\Delta v$, we directly applied the grid to the data cubes and extracted the line profile for each hexagon. We then summed over all channels, multiplying by the channel width of 3 km s$^{-1}$.
Lastly, we calculate $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ by dividing M$_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ by the area of the synthesized beam, expressed in pc$^2$.

evidence.loc: Star formation Efficiency and Gas Depletion Times
evidence.quote: The ratio between $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ and $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ is defined as the star formation efficiency, SFE = $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$/$\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, with units of inverse time (cite: Leroy_2008).
We then summed over all channels, multiplying by the channel width of 3 km s$^{-1}$.

To transform our measurements of CO ($2\rightarrow1$) to CO ($1\rightarrow0$), we used the average ratio reported by (cite: He_2019) for Arp 240, CO ($2\rightarrow1$)/($1\rightarrow0$) = 0.85 $\pm$ 0.02.

To calculate the molecular gas mass, we adopted an $\alpha_{CO}$ value of $1.1$ M$_{\odot}$ (K km s$^{-1}$ pc$^{2}$)$^{-1}$, which is typically used for LIRGs and is close to the values reported by (cite: He_2019) for the brightest regions in CO ($2\rightarrow1$) in Arp 240.

analysis_steps.goal: Measure molecular gas linewidth, turbulent pressure (P_turb), free-fall time (t_ff), and SFE per free-fall time (epsilon_ff)

method.value: Fit single or multiple Gaussian profiles to CO(2-1) spectra in each hexagon using scipy.optimize.leastsq to obtain average sigma linewidth <sigma>, then compute P_turb/k_B (Eq. 6), t_ff (Eq. 8), and epsilon_ff (Eq. 9).

evidence.quote: We identified the number of peaks within each hexagon and modeled them by fitting multiple Gaussian profiles to the spectral-line velocity components. The linewidth of each component was determined by fitting these profiles using $\tt{scipy.optimize.leastsq}$ in Python (cite: SciPy).
For hexagons with multiple components, as shown in the right panel of Figure [6](#fig:lnwith-fit), we use the average of these sigma values to represent the linewidth.

evidence.loc: Free-Fall Time and SFE per Free-Fall Time

analysis_steps.goal: Evaluate distributions and fit the mK-S law slope globally and by morphological component

method.value: Compute skewness and fit 1- and 2-component Gaussian Mixture Models (evaluated with AIC and BIC) to Log Sigma_H2 and Log Sigma_SFR distributions; fit power-law slope N of Log(Sigma_SFR) vs Log(Sigma_H2) using ODR, Linmix (with and without upper limits), and ASURV survival analysis.

evidence.quote: Moreover, we applied the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; (cite: Akaike_74)) and the Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; (cite: Schwarz_78)) to evaluate the fitting of Gaussian Mixture Models (GMMs) to our data.

We used three different fitting algorithms for determining the slope, allowing a comparative analysis of the relation $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$- $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ in Arp 240. These methods include Orthogonal Distance Regression (ODR; (cite: ODR)), which minimizes the orthogonal distances from the data points to the regression line.

The third method uses survival analysis incorporated in the code $\tt{ASURV}$ Rev 1.2 ((cite: ASURV_1990); (cite: Feigelson1992)), which implements the methods presented in (cite: ASURV_1986) for bivariate problems.

key_parameters.value: GMM components = 1 and 2; Linmix MCMC iterations = 10^4

fitting.value: Bayesian MCMC linear regression (Linmix, 10^4 models), Orthogonal Distance Regression (ODR), bivariate survival analysis (ASURV), and Gaussian Mixture Models (scikit-learn).

analysis_steps.goal: Quantify correlations between star formation and kinematic properties and map intensity gradients

method.value: Compute non-parametric Spearman's rank correlation coefficients (rho and p-value) at 16th, 50th, and 84th percentiles between Sigma_H2, Sigma_SFR, SFE and <sigma>, P_turb; compute normalized intensity gradient vectors for CO(2-1) and radio continuum.

evidence.loc: Star Formation and Molecular Gas Kinematics
evidence.quote: Given this non-normality, we utilize the Spearman’s $\rho$ statistic to quantify the correlations.

Indeed, our observations reveal that variations in the intensity of the SFR and molecular gas tracers are not entirely coupled. This is illustrated in Figure [14](#fig:contours), where we explicitly plot the intensity gradients of both tracers.

used_for.value: Data flagging (flagdata), dataset combination (concat), interferometric imaging and automasking (tclean), and rms noise determination (imstat)

evidence.quote: We visually inspected each measurement set and manually removed the defective data, bad antennae, and radio frequency interference (RFI) using the command $\tt{flagdata}$ in CASA (cite: CASA; CASA_2022).
We used $\tt{tclean}$ in CASA v6.5 for imaging, using Briggs weighting and a robust parameter of 0.5.
We determined the root mean square (rms) noise of the radio continuum image by using the $\tt{imstat}$ function in CASA.

used_for.value: Bayesian MCMC linear regression to fit the mK-S law slope accounting for measurement errors, intrinsic scatter, and upper limits

evidence.quote: We also used $\tt{Linmix}$ (cite: Kelly_2007), an approach that accounts for measurement errors in both variables along with their intrinsic scatter and incorporates a Bayesian framework for linear regression.
For $\tt{Linmix}$, the software executes 10$^4$ models using its built-in Markov Chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) routine.

findings_qualitative.value: At 500 pc scales, the mK-S law slope N in Arp 240 is sub-linear globally and for each individual galaxy, regardless of the fitting method.

evidence.quote: In all cases, the slope of the mK-S law at 500 pc scales is sub-linear for this system as well as for its individual galaxies, regardless of the fitting technique employed.

findings_qualitative.value: Arp 240 exhibits two distinct SF modes: bright, compact high-surface-brightness regions with mK-S slopes near unity (N ~ 1), and extended low-surface-brightness regions with shallow slopes.

evidence.quote: We identify two SF regimes: high surface brightness (HSB) regions in RC with N $\sim$1, and low surface brightness (LSB) regions with shallow N (ranging 0.15 $\pm$ 0.09 to 0.48 $\pm$ 0.04).

findings_qualitative.value: Local peaks in the intensity gradients of radio continuum and CO(2-1) are misaligned in some regions (especially the southwestern spiral arm of NGC 5257), decoupling the tracers on 500 pc scales and flattening the mK-S slope.

evidence.quote: Misalignments of local peaks in the intensity gradients of radio continuum and CO (2$\rightarrow$1) emissions, in some regions within both galaxies, weaken the correlation between $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ and $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, resulting in a shallower mK-S slope.

findings_qualitative.value: Sigma_SFR shows no significant correlation with CO(2-1) linewidth at 500 pc scales, but correlates moderately to strongly with turbulent pressure P_turb, while SFE anti-correlates with P_turb outside the brightest regions.

evidence.quote: No significant correlation was found between $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ and CO(2-1) linewidth. However, $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ correlates with P$_{\mathrm{turb}}$, particularly in HSB regions ($\rho >$0.60). In contrast, SF efficiency moderately anti-correlates with P$_{\mathrm{turb}}$ in LSB regions but shows no correlation in HSB regions.

claims.hypothesis: The molecular Kennicutt-Schmidt (mK-S) law maintains a single, nearly linear slope (N ~ 1) when resolved at 500 pc scales across the early-stage galaxy merger Arp 240.
claims.experiment: Measured Sigma_SFR from VLA 3 GHz radio continuum and Sigma_H2 from ALMA CO(2-1) across 341 overlapping 500 pc hexagonal apertures (plus single-tracer detections) and fitted the power-law slope globally and by morphological component using ODR, Linmix, and ASURV.
claims.result: Global mK-S slopes are sub-linear: N = 0.52 +/- 0.17 for Arp 240, 0.52 +/- 0.16 for NGC 5257, and 0.75 +/- 0.15 for NGC 5258; component slopes range from 0.15 +/- 0.09 in low surface brightness arms to 0.98 +/- 0.14 in the nucleus.
claims.finding: Measurements at 500 pc scales do not yield a single linear slope; instead, HSB regions follow N ~ 1 while LSB and decoupled regions exhibit much shallower slopes.

evidence.quote: In Arp 240, N is sub-linear at 0.52 $\pm$ 0.17. For NGC 5257 and NGC 5258, N is 0.52 $\pm$ 0.16 and 0.75 $\pm$ 0.15, respectively. We identify two SF regimes: high surface brightness (HSB) regions in RC with N $\sim$1, and low surface brightness (LSB) regions with shallow N (ranging 0.15 $\pm$ 0.09 to 0.48 $\pm$ 0.04).

evidence.loc: Is there one single slope of the mK-S law?
evidence.quote: These results suggest that measurements at small scales within any particular galaxy do not inherently produce a linear slope (or a single value) for the mK-S law, but rather a range of values dictated by the local ISM conditions.

claims.hypothesis: Spatial decoupling between star formation and molecular gas intensity peaks at 500 pc scales flattens the mK-S slope and inflates apparent star formation efficiency per free-fall time (epsilon_ff).
claims.experiment: Mapped normalized intensity gradient vectors of CO(2-1) and 3 GHz radio continuum across both galaxies and compared local peak alignments with component mK-S slopes and epsilon_ff values.
claims.result: In the southwestern spiral arm of NGC 5257, where CO and radio continuum intensity gradients are strongly misaligned, the mK-S slope is shallow (0.28 +/- 0.18 with Linmix) and 20% of regions exceed epsilon_ff = 100%.
claims.finding: Decoupling between peaks of SF and molecular gas tracers at 500 pc scales weakens the Sigma_SFR-Sigma_H2 correlation, producing shallow slopes and artificially inflating epsilon_ff above 100%.

evidence.quote: Some regions in the periphery of star-forming complexes have faint molecular gas but significant radio continuum, which elevates the $\epsilon_{\mathrm{ff}}$ to values greater than 100%. This highlights how decoupling between tracers can artificially inflate $\epsilon_{\mathrm{ff}}$, creating values that surpass physically plausible thresholds.

Misalignments of local peaks in the intensity gradients of radio continuum and CO (2$\rightarrow$1) emissions, in some regions within both galaxies, weaken the correlation between $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ and $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$, resulting in a shallower mK-S slope.

claims.hypothesis: Star formation rate and efficiency at 500 pc scales in Arp 240 are linked to molecular gas kinematics and regulated by turbulent pressure from stellar feedback.
claims.experiment: Fitted Gaussian linewidths to CO(2-1) spectra, derived turbulent pressure P_turb, and computed Spearman rank correlations between Sigma_H2, Sigma_SFR, SFE and linewidth or P_turb across galaxies and morphological components.
claims.result: Sigma_SFR does not correlate significantly with linewidth (rho = 0.23), correlates positively with P_turb (rho = 0.43 globally; rho = 0.72 in NGC 5258 southern arm and 0.60 in NGC 5257 center), while SFE anti-correlates with P_turb globally (rho = -0.43) and in LSB regions, but shows no correlation in HSB regions.
claims.finding: Immediate feedback injection in HSB gas-rich regions drives strong Sigma_SFR-P_turb correlation while gas abundance drives SF, whereas cumulative feedback in LSB regions regulates SF, producing an inverse SFE-P_turb relation.

evidence.quote: No significant correlation was found between $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ and CO(2-1) linewidth. However, $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$ correlates with P$_{\mathrm{turb}}$, particularly in HSB regions ($\rho >$0.60). In contrast, SF efficiency moderately anti-correlates with P$_{\mathrm{turb}}$ in LSB regions but shows no correlation in HSB regions.
The high density of recent SF in the brightest regions of Arp 240 correlates more strongly with turbulent pressure due to immediate and continuous feedback injection.

why_this_data.value: Arp 240 is an early-stage merger with bright extranuclear SF and no AGN contamination; VLA 3 GHz radio continuum provides the high sensitivity needed to probe both bright compact complexes and diffuse low-surface-brightness ISM without dust attenuation, matched to ALMA CO(2-1) at 500 pc scales.

evidence.quote: The substantial extranuclear star-forming complexes in Arp 240 make this system an ideal laboratory to characterize pure SF in extreme environments with no potential contamination from an AGN.

evidence.loc: Radio Continuum and Star Formation Rates
evidence.quote: We therefore leverage the higher SNR available at 3 GHz to comprehensively calculate the SFR across the full extent of both galaxies, including the low surface brightness ISM, which remains largely undetected at higher frequencies.

why_this_method.value: A uniform hexagonal grid matched to the 1'' beam samples the full extent of both galaxies across surface brightness regimes; three regression methods (ODR, Linmix, ASURV) handle bivariate errors, intrinsic scatter, and non-detection upper limits; Spearman's rho handles non-normal kinematic distributions.

evidence.quote: In this paper, we expand upon these previous studies by employing a uniform grid analysis across the entire extension of both galaxies. This approach allows us to probe regions of both high and low surface brightness in radio continuum and molecular gas.
We used three different fitting algorithms for determining the slope, allowing a comparative analysis of the relation $\Sigma_{\mathrm{SFR}}$- $\Sigma_{\mathrm{H_2}}$ in Arp 240.

evidence.loc: Star Formation and Molecular Gas Kinematics
evidence.quote: Given this non-normality, we utilize the Spearman’s $\rho$ statistic to quantify the correlations.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Using 15 GHz (Ku-Band) or 33 GHz (Ka-Band) radio continuum to trace SFR across the full galaxies was rejected because low surface brightness regions are undetected without at least ten times longer integration times.

evidence.loc: Radio Continuum and Star Formation Rates
evidence.quote: The bright and compact complexes are detected across all frequency bands in our datasets, while the low surface brightness regions are only detected with the 3 GHz. To capture these low surface brightness components at 15 GHz and 33 GHz, observation times would need to be extended to at least ten times those currently utilized at these frequencies to achieve the necessary sensitivity.

alternatives_considered_or_rejected.value: Applying a variable CO-to-H2 conversion factor (alpha_CO) was deferred because 500 pc resolution blends intercloud gas and unresolved velocity gradients, obscuring true cloud-scale (100 pc) variations.

evidence.loc: Velocity Dispersion at 500 pc Scales and alpha_CO
evidence.quote: In light of these complexities, we have opted to apply a uniform value of $\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}}$ in this study, as detailed in $\S$ [3.3](#h2), and defer the analysis of a variable $\alpha_{\mathrm{CO}}$ to a forthcoming paper focused on Arp 240 at approximately 100 pc resolution (Saravia et al. in preparation).

limitations_admitted.value: Assuming a fixed non-thermal spectral index (alpha_NT = -0.85) can locally overestimate the thermal fraction (reaching 0.85 in one hexagon in NGC 5257) and introduces ~20% SFR variation.

evidence.loc: Radio Continuum and Star Formation Rates
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, there is one region in NGC 5257 where the thermal fraction reaches an unusually high value of 0.85, which appears unrealistic.

evidence.loc: Radio Continuum and Star Formation Rates
evidence.quote: For instance, allowing $\alpha_{\mathrm{NT}}$ to vary between $-1$ and $-0.6$ (cite: Murphy_2012), results in a corresponding variation in SFR within $\pm$ 20$\%$.

limitations_admitted.value: At 500 pc spatial resolution, beam smearing, galactic rotation, and blending of multiple GMCs or intercloud gas can broaden measured linewidths and affect turbulent pressure estimates.

evidence.quote: At 500 pc scales, rotation and the blending of individual velocity profiles (e.g., from giant molecules clouds (GMC) or associations of GMCs) are expected to influence the observed linewidths.
However, due to the resolution constraints of our data, some degree of beam smearing may still be present.
It is important to note that this calculation may be affected by residual beam smearing effects, and caution should be exercised when interpreting the results.

limitations_admitted.value: Turbulent pressure calculations assume a constant scale height of 100 pc and a beam filling factor of 1 rather than modeling the vertical gas density distribution.

evidence.quote: We do not attempt to undertake this modeling; instead, we simplify our calculations by assuming a beam filling factor of 1 and adopting a constant scale height of 100 pc throughout our analysis (cite: Leroy_2008; Wilson_2019).

limitations_admitted.value: Current observations lack the angular resolution and radio SED sensitivity in diffuse regions to separate thermal and non-thermal components everywhere or resolve individual 100 pc GMCs.

evidence.loc: What Causes the Decoupling of Molecular Gas and SFR Tracers?
evidence.quote: Under either scenario, our current observations lack the angular resolution and SED sampling needed to fully disentangle the radio continuum emission and probe the distinct characteristics of these two surface brightness regimes.

referee_caveats_inferred: Adopting a single constant alpha_CO = 1.1 M_sun (K km s^-1 pc^2)^-1 across both nuclear/starburst complexes and diffuse spiral arm regions may systematically bias the mK-S slope N if alpha_CO is higher (Milky Way-like) in the lower-density outskirts.

Using 3 GHz radio continuum (dominated by non-thermal synchrotron emission with ~40-100 Myr timescales and cosmic-ray diffusion) at 500 pc scales may smooth out the SFR distribution relative to CO(2-1), artificially flattening the mK-S slope in low surface brightness regions.
Averaging Gaussian sigma values across multiple spectral components within a 500 pc aperture treats distinct velocity components along the line of sight as internal cloud turbulence.

data_public_as_stated.value: ALMA project ID 2015.1.00804.S is cited in the text and Acknowledgements; VLA project codes are referenced via Linden et al. (2019) and Song et al. (2022).

evidence.quote: Our analysis of molecular gas was conducted using the CO ($2\rightarrow1$) transition, employing ALMA pipeline-calibrated datasets (ID 2015.1.00804.S, PI: Kazimierz Sliwa).
A full description of the observations is presented in (cite: Linden_2019) and (cite: Song_2022).
